Description:
Problem:
The trail update command only worked with trails that already had a branch—either by selecting via --branch or defaulting to the current branch. This made it impossible to update branchless trails or to change which branch a trail points at.
Solution:
Added --trail flag to select a trail by number, id, or branch. This is the only way to reach a branchless trail, which has no branch name to match.
Added --set-branch flag to change the trail's branch pointer. For trails that already have a branch, this renames it via the metadata PATCH endpoint. For branchless trails, it attaches a branch through a new /branch endpoint.
Added --branch-action flag to control how a branch is attached to a branchless trail: link (attach an already-pushed branch) or create (backfill it on the forge at the trail's base commit).
New API types TrailBranchRequest and TrailBranchResponse model the /branch endpoint behavior.
Updated the command logic to route --set-branch requests appropriately: POST to /branch for branchless trails (produces output immediately), or fold the branch into the metadata PATCH for existing-branch trails.
Added tests covering branch attachment, response decoding, and flag validation.

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
feat(trail): add --json to trail show, pin the title+body update split

`entire trail show` had no machine-readable output, so an agent could only
read a trail through the human view. It now takes --json and prints one
trail object — the same shape as an entry of `trail list --json`, so both
feed the same parser. The description comes from the detail endpoint the
same way the text view resolves it, and the "-- no description provided --"
placeholder stays out of the JSON: an empty description is an empty string.
A failed description fetch still only warns, and the warning goes to stderr,
so stdout stays parseable.

`entire trail update --title X --body Y` already worked: the server rejects
body and metadata in one PATCH ("Body updates cannot be combined with
metadata updates"), and splitTrailUpdate sends them as two. But nothing
tested that end to end, and splitTrailUpdate decided "this is metadata" by
listing the field names by hand. Adding a metadata field without extending
that list makes the whole update vanish — hasMeta stays false, no PATCH is
sent, and the command still prints success. It now walks the struct
reflectively instead, so a field added later (trail 787's branch rename)
counts as metadata on its own, and a test iterates the struct to keep it
that way.

Also extracts runTrailShowWithClient and runTrailUpdateWithClient so both
paths can be driven against a test server, matching runTrailListAllWithClient.
